# 1 Scope of this vignette

The introductory and multi-omic vignettes describe the core Gaussian and binomial workflows. This vignette documents additional `stablr` capabilities that are easy to miss when reading only the quick-start paths. The topics and the corresponding functions are listed in the table below.

| Topic | Functions |
|-------|-----------|
| Survival STABL | `stabl_fit(family = "cox")` |
| Multinomial classification | `stabl_fit(family = "multinomial")` |
| Artificial features | `artificial_type = "random_permutation"`, `"knockoff"`, `"knockoff_equi"`, `"knockoff_mvr"`, or `NULL` |
| Grouped bootstrap | `groups`, `group_bootstrap_indices()` |
| Reproducibility metrics | `jaccard_similarity()`, `adjusted_similarity()` |
| Disk export | `export_stabl_to_csv()`, `save_stabl_results()` |
| Outer multi-omic CV | `stabl_multiomic_cv()` |
| Cooperative diagnostics | `get_cooperative_features()`, `plot()` on native fits |
| Biomarker interpretation | `stabl_interpret()` |

The examples use small simulated data so that the vignette remains fast during `R CMD check`. The package is loaded as follows.

```{r load}
library(stablr)
```

# 2 Cox proportional-hazards STABL

For time-to-event outcomes, a `survival::Surv` object is passed as `y` and `family = "cox"` is set. Row names of `y` must match `rownames(x)`.

The following commands simulate a small survival dataset with signal in the first two features and construct the lambda grid.

```{r cox-setup}
library(survival)

n <- 80
p <- 15
ids <- paste0("s", seq_len(n))
x_cox <- matrix(
  rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
  dimnames = list(ids, paste0("g", seq_len(p)))
)
# Plant signal in first two features
linpred <- 0.9 * x_cox[, 1] - 0.7 * x_cox[, 2]
y_cox <- Surv(time = rexp(n, exp(linpred)), event = rbinom(n, 1, 0.75))
rownames(y_cox) <- ids

lambda_cox <- auto_lambda_grid(x_cox, y_cox, family = "cox", n_lambda = 8)
```

The linear predictor involves the first two features only, so a stable selection procedure is expected to recover them.

The model is fitted with 40 bootstrap replicates and random-permutation artificial features.

```{r cox-fit}
fit_cox <- stabl_fit(
  x               = x_cox,
  y               = y_cox,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_cox,
  family          = "cox",
  n_bootstraps    = 40L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 42L
)

get_feature_names_out(fit_cox)
head(sort(get_importances(fit_cox), decreasing = TRUE), 6)
```

The output lists the selected feature names, followed by the six features with the largest stability importances. The planted features `g1` and `g2` are expected to rank at the top of the sorted importances.

# 3 Multinomial STABL

Multinomial outcomes use a named factor `y`. The stability matrix has one row per feature, and importances aggregate across classes.

The following commands simulate a three-class problem with weak class signal in the first feature and fit the multinomial model.

```{r multinomial}
n <- 90
p <- 12
ids <- paste0("s", seq_len(n))
x_multi <- matrix(
  rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
  dimnames = list(ids, paste0("m", seq_len(p)))
)
y_multi <- factor(sample(c("A", "B", "C"), n, replace = TRUE), levels = c("A", "B", "C"))
names(y_multi) <- ids
# Weak class signal from first feature
x_multi[y_multi == "B", 1] <- x_multi[y_multi == "B", 1] + 1.5
x_multi[y_multi == "C", 1] <- x_multi[y_multi == "C", 1] - 1.5

lambda_multi <- auto_lambda_grid(x_multi, y_multi, family = "multinomial", n_lambda = 6)

fit_multi <- stabl_fit(
  x               = x_multi,
  y               = y_multi,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_multi,
  family          = "multinomial",
  n_bootstraps    = 30L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 1L
)

get_feature_names_out(fit_multi)
```

The printed vector contains the features selected by the multinomial fit. Because the class signal is confined to feature `m1`, that feature is expected to appear among the selections.

# 4 Knockoff artificial features

The supported artificial-feature settings are `"random_permutation"`, `"knockoff"`, `"knockoff_equi"`, `"knockoff_mvr"`, and `NULL`. `artificial_type = "knockoff"` requests fixed-X knockoffs. `artificial_type = "knockoff_equi"` and `"knockoff_mvr"` request Model-X Gaussian knockoffs when the optional `knockoff` package is installed. All three knockoff modes support at most 3,000 predictors and fail closed above that limit; no chunked construction is claimed to be scientifically valid.

The availability of the `knockoff` package is checked before fitting.

```{r knockoff-check, include = FALSE}
has_knockoff <- requireNamespace("knockoff", quietly = TRUE)
if (!has_knockoff) {
  message("Install the knockoff package to evaluate the knockoff example.")
}
```

When the package is available, a binomial fit with equicorrelated Model-X knockoffs is evaluated.

```{r knockoff-fit, eval = has_knockoff}
n <- 60
p <- 20
ids <- paste0("s", seq_len(n))
x_ko <- matrix(
  rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
  dimnames = list(ids, paste0("k", seq_len(p)))
)
y_ko <- setNames(as.integer(x_ko[, 1] + rnorm(n) > 0), ids)

lambda_ko <- auto_lambda_grid(x_ko, y_ko, family = "binomial", n_lambda = 8)

fit_ko <- stabl_fit(
  x               = x_ko,
  y               = y_ko,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_ko,
  family          = "binomial",
  n_bootstraps    = 30L,
  artificial_type = "knockoff_equi",
  random_state    = 7L
)

get_feature_names_out(fit_ko)
```

The printed vector contains the features selected by the knockoff fit. Feature `k1`, on which the outcome depends, is expected to appear among the selections.

# 5 Grouped bootstrap for repeated measures

When several rows belong to the same subject or batch, a `groups` vector is passed so that bootstrap resampling keeps whole groups together. This prevents leakage across related samples.

The following commands simulate four repeated measurements per subject, inspect one grouped subsample draw, and fit the grouped model.

```{r grouped-bootstrap}
n <- 48
p <- 10
ids <- paste0("s", seq_len(n))
groups <- setNames(rep(paste0("subj", seq_len(12)), each = 4), ids)
x_grp <- matrix(
  rnorm(n * p), nrow = n,
  dimnames = list(ids, paste0("f", seq_len(p)))
)
y_grp <- setNames(rnorm(n) + 0.5 * x_grp[, 1], ids)

# Inspect one grouped draw (whole subjects only)
idx <- group_bootstrap_indices(y_grp, groups = groups, n_subsamples = 24L, seed = 1L)
unique(groups[idx])

lambda_grp <- auto_lambda_grid(x_grp, y_grp, family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 6)

fit_grp <- stabl_fit(
  x               = x_grp,
  y               = y_grp,
  groups          = groups,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_grp,
  family          = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps    = 25L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 3L
)

length(get_feature_names_out(fit_grp))
```

The call to `unique(groups[idx])` prints the subjects entering one subsample; each subject appears either with all four of its rows or not at all. The final line reports the number of features selected by the grouped Gaussian fit.

The same `groups` argument is forwarded by `stabl_multiomic_train_validate()` and `stabl_multiomic_cv()` for outer fold construction.

Classification bootstraps redraw subsamples until at least two observations per class are present. This slightly biases the subsample distribution relative to vanilla STABL; the deviation is deliberate and documented, and it buys class-diverse subsamples.

# 6 Reproducibility across repeated fits

Selection-stability metrics compare feature lists from repeated STABL runs. Jaccard similarity is the simplest overlap measure, and adjusted similarity corrects for chance overlap when set sizes differ.

Two fits with different random states are compared first, and a pairwise similarity matrix across four seeds is computed afterwards.

```{r reproducibility}
run_once <- function(seed) {
  stabl_fit(
    x = x_grp, y = y_grp, groups = groups,
    lambda_grid = lambda_grp,
    family = "gaussian",
    n_bootstraps = 20L,
    artificial_type = "random_permutation",
    random_state = seed
  )
}

fit_a <- run_once(11L)
fit_b <- run_once(22L)
sel_a <- get_feature_names_out(fit_a)
sel_b <- get_feature_names_out(fit_b)

jaccard_similarity(sel_a, sel_b)
adjusted_similarity(sel_a, sel_b, nb_total_elements = ncol(x_grp))

# Pairwise matrix across several seeds
fits <- lapply(11:14, run_once)
sels <- lapply(fits, get_feature_names_out)
jaccard_matrix(sels)
```

The first two printed values are the Jaccard and the adjusted similarity between the selections from seeds 11 and 22. The matrix at the end gives the pairwise Jaccard similarities for the fits with seeds 11 to 14; off-diagonal values close to 1 indicate selections that are robust to the random state.

# 7 Exporting results to disk

`export_stabl_to_csv()` writes stability-score tables for a single-omic fit. `save_stabl_results()` bundles scores, diagnostics, selected-feature tables, and feature-distribution figures for a full analysis folder. It writes `STABL scores.csv`, `Max STABL scores.csv`, `FDR Graph.<fmt>`, `Stability Path.<fmt>`, `Selected Features/Selected features.csv`, and `Selected Features/Feature distributions.<fmt>` when the relevant diagnostics and selected features are available.

The following commands write the score tables and the full results bundle to a temporary directory.

```{r export, eval = FALSE}
# File-writing path; exercised by tests/testthat/test-phase7.R.
tmp <- tempfile("stablr_export")
dir.create(tmp)

export_stabl_to_csv(fit_grp, path = file.path(tmp, "grp"))
list.files(file.path(tmp, "grp"))

save_stabl_results(
  object     = fit_grp,
  path       = file.path(tmp, "bundle"),
  x          = x_grp,
  y          = y_grp,
  task_type  = "regression",
  figure_fmt = "png",
  override   = TRUE
)
```

The chunk is not evaluated during the vignette build, so no files are written when the package is checked.

# 8 Outer cross-validation for multi-omic workflows

When no fixed validation split exists, `stabl_multiomic_cv()` runs STABL, and optional fusion branches, on rotating outer folds. Cooperative fusion is supported in this function; nested CV (`stabl_multiomic_nested_cv()`) does not forward cooperative mode.

A two-omic Gaussian fit with cooperative fusion and three outer folds is specified as follows.

```{r outer-cv}
n <- 50
ids <- paste0("s", seq_len(n))
x_a <- matrix(rnorm(n * 8), nrow = n, dimnames = list(ids, paste0("a", 1:8)))
x_b <- matrix(rnorm(n * 8), nrow = n, dimnames = list(ids, paste0("b", 1:8)))
y_cv <- setNames(0.6 * x_a[, 1] - 0.4 * x_b[, 2] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3), ids)

lambda_cv <- list(
  omic_a = auto_lambda_grid(x_a, y_cv, family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 5),
  omic_b = auto_lambda_grid(x_b, y_cv, family = "gaussian", n_lambda = 5)
)

cv_fit <- stabl_multiomic_cv(
  x_list          = list(omic_a = x_a, omic_b = x_b),
  y               = y_cv,
  lambda_grid     = lambda_cv,
  v               = 3L,
  family          = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps    = 15L,
  artificial_type = "random_permutation",
  random_state    = 5L,
  cooperative_fusion = TRUE,
  rho             = c(0, 0.3),
  cooperation_nfolds = 3L
)

head(cv_fit$diagnostics)
if (!is.null(cv_fit$fold_results[[1]]$cooperative_fusion)) {
  get_cooperative_features(cv_fit$fold_results[[1]])
}
```

The head of the diagnostics data frame summarises each omic and fold. When the first fold contains a cooperative branch, `get_cooperative_features()` prints the features selected by the cooperative model in that fold.

# 9 Cooperative coefficient paths

The built-in cooperative engine registers `plot.multiview()` for fitted cooperative models. After a cooperative workflow, the selected fit object lives in `$cooperative_fusion$fit`.

A cooperative fit on the OOL training data is run and plotted as follows.

```{r cooperative-plot, fig.alt = "Cooperative coefficient paths by view"}
ool <- load_ool_data(split = "train")
lambda_ool <- list(
  cytof = auto_lambda_grid(ool$x_list$cytof, ool$y, n_lambda = 6),
  proteomics = auto_lambda_grid(ool$x_list$proteomics, ool$y, n_lambda = 6)
)

coop_fit <- stabl_multiomic_train_validate(
  x_train_list       = ool$x_list,
  y_train            = ool$y,
  lambda_grid        = lambda_ool,
  family             = "gaussian",
  n_bootstraps       = 12L,
  artificial_type    = "random_permutation",
  random_state       = 42L,
  cooperative_fusion = TRUE,
  rho                = 0.3,
  cooperation_nfolds = 3L
)

cf <- coop_fit$cooperative_fusion
get_cooperative_diagnostics(coop_fit)
plot(cf$fit)
```

The printed diagnostics summarise the cooperative fit, and the plot displays the coefficient paths of the fitted multiview model. Features whose paths persist over a wide range of lambda values are the candidates for stable cross-view selection.

# 10 Interpreting a fitted selection

A STABL fit answers one question: which features are stable. It does not
answer three others. How large is each effect? Which features are redundant?
How much does the fitted model rely on each feature? `stabl_interpret()`
answers these three questions for an existing fit. It does not re-run STABL.

The function returns one evidence table. Each row is a feature. The columns
record four separate dimensions: the stability score, a conditional signed
effect, a correlation group, and a permutation importance. These dimensions
are different quantities. They are never merged into one score.

```{r interpretation}
set.seed(11L)
n <- 120
x <- matrix(rnorm(n * 8), n, 8,
            dimnames = list(paste0("s", 1:n), paste0("f", 1:8)))
# f1 and f2 are correlated substitutes; f3 is an independent signal.
x[, "f2"] <- x[, "f1"] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
y <- setNames(0.9 * x[, "f1"] + 0.7 * x[, "f3"] + rnorm(n, sd = 0.6),
              rownames(x))

fit <- stabl_fit(x, y, lambda_grid = data.frame(lambda = c(0.3, 0.1, 0.05)),
                 n_bootstraps = 30L, artificial_type = "random_permutation",
                 random_state = 11L)
ins <- stabl_interpret(fit, x, y, family = "gaussian", n_repeats = 10L,
                       random_state = 12L)
summary(ins)[, c("feature", "stability", "coefficient", "effect_direction",
                 "correlation_group", "permutation_importance")]
```

Three readings matter. First, a feature can be highly stable yet have a
small conditional effect. This happens when a correlated substitute shares
the signal. Second, the correlation group flags such substitutes. It is a
grouping of observed biomarkers, not a claim of biological equivalence.
Third, the permutation importance is apparent: it is measured on the fitting
data, so it is optimistic. All effects and importances here are
post-selection and descriptive. They are not selection-adjusted inference.
